newsitem.title: UK: O&M, JWT to combine media divisions by end 1998.
newsitem.headline: O&M, JWT to combine media divisions by end 1998.

text.p: Ogilvy & Mather and J. Walter Thompson, global advertising agencies owned by WPP Group Plc , plan to merge their media operations by the end of 1998, the head of O&M in the UK said on Monday.
But Tom Bury, the chief executive and deputy chairman of O&M in London, told Reuters the merger would only work well if it provided clients with added value and not simply greater volume.
"It will happen in calendar 1998 without a doubt," he said in an interview, when asked about news reports predicting O&M and JWT would combine their media operations.
The media divisions of O&M and JWT carry out media planning and media buying, which means they advise companies on where to spend their advertising budgets and then they book the advertising space.
Any such merger by O&M and JWT would address a couple of hot issues facing the advertising industry.
The first is how agencies with costly global networks can create better synergy with sister organisations.
O&M and JWT are two of the biggest global networks in the world and among some 40 advertising and marketing services companies owned by WPP.

A lack of sufficient synergy led Cordiant Plc, another London-based advertising holding company, to announce in April that it would demerge its ad agencies, Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising and Bates Worldwide.

The second issue with which ad agencies are grappling is how to compete with so-called media independents -- companies that specialise in doing media planning and media buying but are not part of ad agencies.

Martin Sorrell, chief executive of WPP, the world's biggest advertising and marketing services group, said recently ad agencies were losing business in Europe to media independents like Carat, which is owned by London-based Aegis Group Plc , and CIA Group Plc.
Tom Bury also told Reuters O&M in the UK had welcomed a trend by some of its clients to pay O&M on a flexible fee basis rather than by commission.
Client companies have traditionally paid their ad agencies commissions calculated at 15 percent of the total amount clients spend on advertising space.
Many clients have said in recent years they prefered paying by fees because that supposedly made ad agencies more accountable, but the shakeup in the method of payment has upset many ad agencies.
But Bury said, "We don't mind either (fees or commissions). We love fees."

He said about 50 percent of O&M's business in the UK was now paid for by fees and 50 percent by commission, compared to five years ago, when it was about 20 percent in fees and 80 percent in commission.

He said he expected the trend to continue, with a possible two-thirds of O&M's business in the UK eventually paid for by fees and one-third by commission. He said O&M was trying hard to be accountable to clients and was "committed to total transparency on numbers" since the agency was always ready to show clients the costs that went into creating ads.
Some big advertisers have complained in the last few years that their ad agencies were not financially transparent enough.
Several ad agencies have also been losing business to management consultancies which not only advise companies on financial matters, but now increasingly advise on branding and communications issues.

Bury said he saw competition with management consultancies as an opportunity for O&M, which had begun hiring more people with MBAs -- Masters in Business Administration -- and was itself being hired by more and more clients to do business consultancy.
"No consultants have taken any business from me yet. We have clients who pay us for consulting...We look very hard for people with business degrees," he said.
Bury said O&M had invested a lot of money in information technology at its office at Canary Wharf to keep pace with the changing nature of the advertising business.
He said executives at O&M who used to get a central information department to do research on consumer markets and other areas now very often did the research themselves on their own computers.
Bury said he hoped O&M, which was the third biggest agency in the UK in 1996 in terms of billings, after Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO and J Walter Thompson, would climb to second place for 1997.
O&M's billings reached 254.63 million pounds ($427.5 million) in 1996, according to AC Nielsen Meal.
"I'd be disappointed if we weren't second by the end of the year," he said. -- London Advertising Newsdesk +44 171 542 2792 ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
